title: A Bell for the House
premise: Theo Yarrow, a pest controller who has spent twelve years rationalizing the unexplained, returns to their childhood home after their mother's death and finds Wren — the imaginary friend they buried in memory — waiting on the porch, unchanged since age nine. The house's old hand-bell rings on its own each night at 3:07 a.m., summoning the drowned children of Bellows Well to finish a song that was interrupted mid-verse when the town hushed up a drowning a century ago. Theo learns the song's final verse from Wren, but singing it wrong means joining the chorus forever; they must instead give the verse to the well itself before it refills with rainwater and the dead rise wet-handed into the house. In the end Theo rings the bell themselves, names the drowned child the town erased, and lets the house go quiet — inheriting not the property but the debt of remembering.
about_author: Quentin Delacroix is the pen name of a former rural building inspector who spent a decade documenting condemned houses across the American Midwest. They write horror about structures that remember what people prefer to forget.

chapters.title: The Call Sheet
chapters.summary: Theo takes a routine pest-control call to 14 Hollow Lane — the address they grew up in — now legally theirs after their mother's death. POV: Theo. Beat: dread disguised as professionalism; they almost turn the truck around.

chapters.title: Something With Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Inspecting the cellar, Theo finds greasy child-sized prints ascending the inside of the sealed well cap, fresh despite decades of closure. POV: Theo. Beat: the first crack in twelve years of rational explanations.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: At dusk, Wren — Theo's imaginary friend, aged nine forever — sits on the porch swing, patient as furniture. POV: Theo. Beat: vertigo of recognition; grief for the childhood self who invented him.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Sorting their mother's belongings, Theo finds her journals: forty years of entries logging the bell's ringing, the well's sounds, and her attempts to keep 'it fed with attention.' POV: Theo. Beat: betrayal and tenderness entangled — she knew and stayed silent.

chapters.title: 3:07 A.M.
chapters.summary: The hand-bell in the hallway rings by itself; through the floorboards comes humming in several small voices, one verse short of complete. POV: Theo. Beat: terror sharpening into curiosity — the song wants finishing.

chapters.title: Bellows Well
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Theo reads the 1898 account: a girl named Adeline Crowe drowned in the well during a school song game, and the town sang the last verse over her grave once, then never again. POV: Theo. Beat: cold anger at how neatly justice was buried.

chapters.title: What Wren Remembers
chapters.summary: Wren admits he isn't imaginary — he is what Adeline's unfinished verse left behind, wearing a shape a lonely child could love. POV: Theo. Beat: heartbreak; the friend was always a haunting, and also always kind.

chapters.title: The Verse That Isn't There
chapters.summary: The children's song appears in a folklore collection with its final stanza redacted by the compiler 'at the family's request.' Theo realizes the family was paid off. POV: Theo. Beat: inheritance reframed — the house came with an obligation attached.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Look Away
chapters.summary: Theo canvasses longtime residents; doors close, one old man whispers that his grandmother helped fill the well and died humming. POV: Theo. Beat: isolation — the whole town is complicit in the silence.

chapters.title: Rain Coming
chapters.summary: A storm front stalls over the valley; the well begins to refill, and the humming grows wetter, closer, syllables surfacing like bubbles. POV: Theo. Beat: countdown pressure — the deadline is weather.

chapters.title: Mother's Last Entry
chapters.summary: The journal's final pages reveal Theo's mother met Wren too, as a girl, and chose silence to protect Theo — feeding the haunting attention so it wouldn't take a child instead. POV: Theo. Beat: devastating reframe of maternal love as bargain.

chapters.title: Learning It Wrong
chapters.summary: Wren teaches Theo the melody but refuses the words; Theo hums along once and their reflection sings ahead of them. POV: Theo. Beat: body-horror intimacy — the song colonizes anyone who carries it carelessly.

chapters.title: The Drowned Choir
chapters.summary: Night: figures stand hip-deep in the flooded cellar, mouths open, waiting for a verse only the living can carry. Theo flees upstairs and nails the door. POV: Theo. Beat: siege horror; the house is no longer shelter.

chapters.title: Adeline Crowe's Granddaughter
chapters.summary: Theo tracks down Adeline's last living descendant, who possesses a locked hymnal said to hold the true verse — and a family curse of humming in sleep. POV: Theo. Beat: alliance forged in shared inherited guilt.

chapters.title: The Hymnal
chapters.summary: Opening the hymnal releases a smell of well water; the verse is written backward, meant to be given away, never kept. The granddaughter begs Theo to take it. POV: Theo. Beat: burden transferred — knowledge as contagion.

chapters.title: Seduction of the Chorus
chapters.summary: Exhausted, Theo dreams of the choir promising rest, belonging, their mother's voice among them; waking, they find mud on their bare feet and the cellar door open. POV: Theo. Beat: temptation — the dead offer what grief starves.

chapters.title: Wren's Confession
chapters.summary: Wren reveals the trap: whoever sings the verse aloud becomes the new keeper, bound to the house as he is. He taught Theo out of loneliness, then repented. POV: Theo. Beat: rage, then forgiveness — even hauntings can be cowardly and sorry.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: The storm breaks; water climbs the stairs, and the choir rises with it, reaching the kitchen where the bell hangs silent, waiting for a hand. POV: Theo. Beat: climax pressure — nowhere left to run, only a choice.

chapters.title: Ringing It Themselves
chapters.summary: Instead of singing, Theo seizes the bell, speaks Adeline's name and the verse aloud as testimony — not song but accusation — ringing once per line, giving the words to the well rather than the air. POV: Theo. Beat: climax — justice outside law, memory as verdict.

chapters.title: The Water Gives Back
chapters.summary: The well drains with a long exhalation; small shapes bow and dissolve, and Wren, finally aging, thanks Theo and goes with them. POV: Theo. Beat: catharsis — the haunting ends not in banishment but release.

chapters.title: Estate Sale
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Theo sells the house to a young family and leaves the bell with a written history of Adeline Crowe, refusing to let the record go quiet again. POV: Theo. Beat: bittersweet inheritance — passing on truth instead of silence.

chapters.title: Humming Down the Highway
chapters.summary: Driving away, Theo catches themselves humming the completed song and stops, letting the silence hold — until, faintly, somewhere far behind, a porch swing creaks in time. POV: Theo. Beat: ambiguous resolution — some songs are finished, some merely resting.
